en: *An Essay on the Balanced Mind Regarding the Three Teachings*, Volume One,
composed by the Scholar of Jingzhai, Liu Mi.
I have observed that China has possessed the Three Teachings since the Lord Fu Xi drew the eight trigrams.
Confucianism began from this point.
From the time Laozi authored the *Daode jing*,
Daoism began from this point.
Since Emperor Ming of the Han dynasty dreamed of the golden man,
Buddhism first began here;
this is the sequence of the Three Teachings in China.
In general, the Confucians establish their teachings through rectitude;
the Daoists establish their teachings through veneration;
and the Buddhists establish their teachings through the Great [Vehicle].
To observe their love for life and hatred of killing is to see that they share the same benevolence;
to regard others as oneself is to see that they share the same impartiality.
To curb anger, stifle desire, prohibit excess, and prevent wrongdoing constitutes the same practice of cultivation.
Yet, to the thunder it is as if all were deaf;
to the sun and moon, they are as if all were blind.
Thus, the customs and transformations are one and the same.
Judging from these coarse traces,
the principles of the world do not exceed this.
Although there are two paths— good and evil—
the intent of the Three Teachings is nothing other than to desire that people return to goodness. Thus,
Emperor Xiaozong composed the "Discourse on Distinguishing the Origin of the Way," in which he said:
Use Buddhism to govern the mind;
use the Way (Daoism) to govern the body;
use Confucianism to govern the world.
If one truly knows that the mind, the body,
and the world cannot tolerate even a single one of these being left ungoverned,
then how could the Three Teachings tolerate even a single one of them being left unestablished?
The Layman Wujin composed the *Treatise on Protecting the Dharma*, stating:
"Confucianism treats the skin;
Daoism treats the blood vessels."
The Buddha heals the marrow and bones;
he truly knows the skin, the blood vessels, and the marrow,
such that there is not a single part that he does not heal.
Thus, among the three teachings, how could there be even one that is not put into practice?
In China, the Confucian teaching ensures that the fundamental social relations are rectified and the human ethics are clarified.
Ritual, music, law, and government reach all quarters without contradiction;
thus heaven and earth, and all things therein, find their proper positions and receive their nourishment.
Their contribution to the world is truly great.
Therefore, although the First Emperor of Qin wished to eliminate the Confucians,
the Confucians could ultimately not be eliminated.
As for the Daoist teachings in China:
It causes people to maintain themselves through purity and emptiness, and to sustain themselves through humility and weakness.
It thoroughly washes away the habits of worldly entanglement and confusion,
leading them back to the realm of stillness, silence, and non-action.
Its contribution to the teachings of the world is indeed ultimate. Thus,
when Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty sought to eliminate the Way,
the Way ultimately could not be eliminated.
In China, Buddhism causes people to abandon the ornate for the substantial,
and turn their backs on the false to return to the true.
From the stage of practice through effort, one attains the stage of established practice;
from self-benefit, one proceeds to the benefit of others.
Thus, one becomes that upon which the people of the world rely and take refuge.
There is nothing that can surpass this. Thus,
although the rulers of the three Wu dynasties sought to extinguish Buddhism,
Buddhism ultimately could not be extinguished.
Regarding Li Shiqian of the Sui dynasty’s discourse on the Three Teachings,
he stated that Buddhism is the sun, Daoism is the moon, and Confucianism is the five planets.
Is this not because these three luminaries exist in the heavens, and it would be impossible for even one to be missing?
Furthermore, the three teachings existing in the world are likewise indispensable;
though they differ in their relative merits,
it is essential that none be neglected.
However, people have differing minds,
and their minds hold differing views;
those who aspire to the Way say:
The Buddha is no less venerable than the Way.
Those who turn toward the Buddha say that the Way is no greater than the Buddha.
The Confucians maintain their own integrity with rectitude;
furthermore, they concurrently denounce Daoism and Buddhism as heterodox teachings.
Right and wrong have been muddled and confused for a thousand years;
I shall clarify and distinguish them.
I believe that one must not judge with a private mind,
nor judge with a heart of love or hatred; rather,
one must level the mind and contemplate the ultimate achievement.
Then one can achieve a sudden, clear resolution, like ice melting away.
For the "ultimate achievement" (*jigong*) is the point where causes are gathered and results are realized.
Among all things and events in the world, each possesses its own ultimate achievement.
"Splashing the body with mud and smearing the feet with dust is the business of the plowman;
yet it leads to the granaries being filled to capacity."
This is the ultimate achievement of the farmer.
To travel on foot through the weeds and sleep under the open sky is the business of the merchant.
As for filling a basket with gold,
this represents the ultimate achievement of a merchant;
the same applies to the Three Teachings.
The Confucian has the ultimate achievement of Confucianism;
the Daoist has the ultimate achievement of Daoism;
the Buddhist has the ultimate achievement of Buddhism.
If one examines their relative merits based on their ultimate achievements,
there are certain things that become clear without the need for further discernment.
Judging from this present perspective:
The teaching of the Confucian school proceeds from the individual to the family,
and from the family to the state.
From a single state, it was extended to the four seas and filled the six directions;
this may be called "maintaining the concise while dispensing widely.
As for that which lies beyond the four seas and the six directions—
What, then, was it like?
The account says:
it spread eastward and reached westward, extending as far as the four seas.
This is the ultimate limit, extending no further than the four seas; it ends here,
and there is nowhere else to go.
This is precisely the teaching of the Confucian school. Therefore,
those who study Confucianism preserve their minds,
nourish their natures, tread upon benevolence, and practice righteousness.
He was a man of pure integrity who fully embodied the Way and possessed all virtues;
yet when these were manifested in his administration and applied to his undertakings,
they were capable of bringing his sovereign to the heights of excellence.
It can bring moisture and benefit to the people;
it can stabilize the state and establish the altars of soil and grain;
it can support the teachings of the world and bring about great peace.
When one’s merit is accomplished and the body grows old,
one’s name remains in the annals of history;
such is the ultimate achievement of the Confucian.
Zengzi said:
"To wait until death before ceasing—is that not too remote?
For when one reaches death, it is the ultimate limit."
The teaching of the Daoist school extends from one's own person to the realm of the unseen and transcends from the human world to the heavens above.
From the mountain forests and rocky caves up to the vast and boundless Dàluó Heaven and the towering Jīnquè Palace,
one may be said to have transcended the mundane and entered the realm of the sages.
As for that which lies beyond the creative transformations of heaven and earth—
What then is the case?
The explanation says:
"The great realm of heaven is as minute as a fine mote of dust."
This is extremely vast, yet it does not exceed the limits of the celestial sphere;
the realm is thus confined to this,
and that which lies beyond it—
This is not something to be known through conventional cognition;
such is the teaching of the Daoists.
Therefore, those who study the Dao—
With the spirit concentrated and movements in harmony with the formless,
one stands poised in a state of purity and few desires,
exhaling the old and inhaling the new while accumulating merit and refining conduct.
One may achieve liberation through the corpse; one may ascend on wings.
One may employ ghosts and spirits and summon wind and rain;
one may assist in the transformation of creation and establish profound merit.
An infinite lifespan and sovereign bliss—
such is the ultimate achievement of the Way.
As the *Huangting jing* says:
"Attaining longevity and eternal vision, one then soars away.
This indeed represents the ultimate limit of longevity;
such is the teaching of the Buddhist school.
When a single Buddha appears,
he takes the trichiliocosm as his land of retribution.
To speak of this using just one world as an illustration:
Within a single world-system there is Mount Sumeru,
which rises from the great ocean to stand aloft in the high heavens;
the sun and moon revolve around its mid-slope.
Thus day and night are divided.
On the four sides of Mount Sumeru are the four continents.
The eastern one is called Pūrvavideha.
The west is called Aparagoyānī;
the south is called Jambudvīpa;
and the north is called Uttarakuru.
Within each of the four great continents,
there are three thousand islands. This present world is Jambudvīpa.
This present Middle Kingdom is but one of the three thousand continents within Jambudvīpa.
Śākyamuni descended to be born in India.
This is precisely the center of Jambudvīpa.
The places on the four sides of Mount Sumeru where the sun and moon appear above are called the Heaven of Śakra.
Furthermore, above the void it dwells in brilliant clarity.
The four layers of cloud-banks above are collectively named the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Above those, the eighteen layers of cloud-banks are collectively named the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*).
Furthermore, the four tiers of heavens above the empty space are collectively named the Formless Realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
Within these three realms, all classes of sentient beings undergo birth, old age, sickness, and death;
this constitutes a single world-system.
One thousand such world-systems are called a small chiliocosm.
One thousand such small chiliocosms are called a medium chiliocosm.
This is one million.
A thousand such medium chiliocosms are called a great trichiliocosm.
This refers to one hundred *koṭis*.
Because the word "thousand" is stated three times,
it is called a "trichiliocosm" (three-thousandfold great thousandfold world system).
In fact, there is one great trichiliocosm.
Within this one great trichiliocosm, there are ten billion Mount Sumerus, ten billion suns and moons, and ten billion sets of four continents—
like a million strings of small coins.
Place one coin in each realm;
when these one million strings of cash are exhausted,
it constitutes a great trichiliocosm.
This is the reward-land of a single Buddha.
When one Buddha appears,
there are ten billion bodies within ten billion worlds.
They appear simultaneously.
Thus, the Brahmajāla Sūtra says:
"Upon a single flower, there are ten billion lands."
In each land there is one Śākyamuni;
each sits beneath a Bodhi tree and simultaneously attains the Way of Buddhahood.
In this manner, there are thousands of billions [of forms] of the original body of Vairocana,
and thousands of billions of Śākyamunis.
Each one receives a multitude as numerous as motes of dust;
this is what is called the manifestation of a thousand times ten million transformation bodies.
By means of these thousand times ten million transformation bodies, [he acts].

And he transforms and delivers those within hundreds of thousands of millions of worlds—those born from wombs, eggs, moisture, or by transformation; those without feet, with two feet, four feet, or many feet; those with form or without form; those with perception or without perception, up to those who are neither with nor without perception.
To cause all to attain deliverance—
this is the teaching of the Buddha’s house. Therefore,
those who study Buddhism [should act accordingly].
Realize that the five aggregates are all empty;
clarify the purity of the six sense faculties;
distance oneself from the ten unwholesome actions and practice the ten wholesome ones.
By contemplating the four foundations of mindfulness and practicing the four right efforts,
one eliminates the sixty-two views,
leaving no room for falsehood or deception.
He severed the ninety-eight latent tendencies (*anuśaya*),
so that no afflictions (*kleśa*) could disturb him;
he scrupulously observed all three thousand modes of deportment and eighty thousand subtle practices without exception.
One constantly cultivates the four immeasurable minds and the six perfections. Within this practice,
one forgets one's own body for the sake of the Dharma—
just as [the ancients] carved scriptures by slicing their skin and piercing their flesh, or severed their arms and cast themselves down to seek instruction.
Without fear or doubt,
one forgets oneself for the sake of others;
thus, it is like enduring suffering to cut off one's own flesh to feed a hawk, or sacrificing one's life to provide one's body as fodder for a tiger.
Without fear or dread,
they cast aside wealth, treasures, kingdoms, cities, wives,
and children as if they were worn-out sandals.
He relinquishes his limbs, hands, feet, head, eyes, marrow,
and brain as if casting them off;
from birth to birth, he passes through hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of lifetimes.
Yet this mind does not regress;
from kalpa to kalpa, passing through hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of kalpas,
this mind becomes ever more diligent.
Thus, through the fulfillment of the fruits of the three *asaṃkhyeya*-kalpas and the perfection of the merit of ten thousand virtues, one is free from the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*).
As for these four propositions:
it is said that all phenomena do not arise from themselves.
Nor does it arise from another;
it is neither co-existent nor causeless.
Therefore, it is said that non-arising cuts off the hundred negations;
one penetrates immeasurable and boundless dharma-gates and skillfully enters immeasurable and boundless samādhis.
He achieves the five faculties and the five powers;
he is fully endowed with the three types of supernormal knowledge and the three insights;
and he perfectly manifests the four wisdoms and the three bodies.
They have transcended to realize the six supernormal powers and the five eyes;
having attained the four kinds of unimpeded eloquence, they preach the Dharma without end;
and having entered the four bases of power, their spiritual penetrations are sovereign.
The eight bases of mastery and the eight liberations are constantly manifested;
the four fearlessnesses and the four means of integration are enjoyed without exhaustion;
as are the eight branches of the noble path and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
It is not equal to the three vehicles;
it is the subtle and wondrous Dharma-body, adorned with the thirty-two marks and eighty secondary characteristics.
Throughout kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the past and kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the future, there is nothing he does not see clearly.
Regarding the present, throughout worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, there is no mind among sentient beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges that he does not fully know.
The Honored One of the Ten Epithets, Perfectly Radiant,
who transcends the three realms above;
this is the All-Knowing Wisdom.
He is the God among gods;
he is the Unsurpassed Dharma King;
he is the Truly and Fully Enlightened One who transcends all skillful means and has perfected the Ten Powers.
Returning to deliver all sentient beings throughout the dharma-realm—
such is the ultimate achievement of a Buddha.
As the Lotus Sūtra says:
The Tathāgata appears in the world for the sake of one great cause and condition:
he universally desires to enable all sentient beings to together accomplish this Way.
This is due to his great vow and great power.
"I vow that all sentient beings shall together realize the sublime fruit of unsurpassed nirvana.
For this reason, one who discerns the three teachings...
One must not deliberate with a private mind;
one must not deliberate with a heart of love or hatred.
Only by leveling the mind and contemplating its ultimate efficacy can one arrive at the truth.
Thus we know that when those in the world who study Confucianism reach the point of gathering causes and bringing forth results,
they do nothing more than seek fame and office.
Among those in the world who study the Way,
when they reach the point where causes are gathered and results are realized,
it does not exceed the attainment of longevity.
When those in this world who study the Buddha reach the point where causes are gathered and results are realized,
they shall be able to sever birth and death, attain ultimate nirvana, universally deliver all sentient beings, and together achieve perfect enlightenment.
Is their superiority or inferiority not clearly visible?
Therefore, let me attempt a comparison.
That which is practiced by the Confucian school—
China is also [a place] where Daoism is practiced;
it encompasses both the heavens and the human realm.
The sphere of practice for Buddhism extends throughout the entirety of empty space and pervades the entire Dharma-realm;
whereas Confucianism governs but a single family, its authority being exercised only within the boundaries of its own walls.
As for what lies beyond the boundary walls,
it cannot be summoned by proclamation;
yet the Way is like a magistrate governing a single district, whose administration and teachings reach throughout the four borders.
As for those beyond the four borders,
they cannot be brought under control;
yet the Buddha has encompassed the four seas as the sovereign of the world.
Under the vast heavens and throughout all lands, there are none who are not my subjects and people;
rites, music, military expeditions, and punishments all issue from me alone.
This is the distinction between the breadth and narrowness of the Three Teachings.
Those who study Confucianism cease their efforts only after death;
this is a matter spanning a hundred years.
Those who study the Way strive to seek longevity.
This spans millions of years.
Those who study the Buddha-dharma and wish to sever birth and death to abide in profound stillness must pass through kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, without end.
The Confucian way is like a single lamp illuminating a single night;
when the bell tolls and the water-clock runs out, the oil is exhausted and the lamp goes out.
The Way [of the Buddha] is like King Ajātaśatru’s hundred-year lamp that illuminated the Buddha’s śarīra.
After a hundred years have passed, the lamp will eventually extinguish;
yet the Buddha remains like the bright sun, illuminating the ten thousand ages with eternal clarity,
setting in the west and rising in the east in an unceasing cycle.
This is the distinction between the antiquity and recency of these three teachings.
By this, one knows that there are mundane dharmas and supramundane dharmas:
the two teachings of Confucianism and Daoism are mundane dharmas.
Buddhism begins with worldly dharmas and concludes with supramundane dharmas.
Why is it called "worldly"?
The Avataṃsaka Sūtra states:
"There is the world of devas, the world of humans, and the world of King Yama;
these are within the three realms."
All these are called the world.
There is a phenomenon herein that causes people to revolve through birth and death in an endless cycle.
That which does not transcend the interior of the triple world is called mundane phenomena (*lokadharma*).
The single true nature of awakening (*ekasatyabodhikṣaṇa*) encompasses the ten directions within its embrace.
That which cannot be bound by the three realms is called the supramundane dharma.
The Buddha established his teachings through the five vehicles.
The first two vehicles, namely the Human Vehicle and the Celestial Vehicle,
pertain to worldly dharmas. The latter three vehicles, namely the Śrāvaka, Pratyekabuddha, and Bodhisattva Vehicles, pertain to the supramundane.
These are supramundane dharmas.
The Vehicle of Humans refers to the five precepts.
The first is called non-killing.
This means that when love arises,
one must not recklessly harm even a single creature;
it does not stop at merely abstaining from eating their flesh.
The second is non-stealing.
This means not taking what is not rightfully one's own,
nor seizing or pilfering the property of others.
The third is refraining from sexual misconduct.
This means not being promiscuous with those who are not one's lawful spouse.
The fourth is refraining from false speech,
which means not deceiving others with one's words.
The fifth is refraining from drinking alcohol.
That is to say, one does not allow intoxication to disturb the cultivation of the mind.
By maintaining these five,
one is thereby provided with the means to become a true person.
The Five Constant Virtues of Confucianism are precisely its intended meaning.
The "vehicle of Heaven" refers to the Ten Wholesome Actions.
The first is non-killing.
2. Not stealing.
3. Not engaging in sexual misconduct.
4. Not speaking falsely.
The meaning of these four is the same as that of the five precepts.
The fifth is called "avoiding frivolous speech," which means not using words to gloss over one's faults.
The sixth is refraining from double-tongued speech;
that is, speaking to people in their presence rather than behind their backs.
The seventh is refraining from harsh speech.
That is to say, not reviling others;
it is also called not speaking what is unrighteous.
The eighth is not being envious.
That is to say, being free from envy and jealousy. Ninth is non-anger,
which means not harboring resentment within the mind.
The tenth is non-delusion,
which means not being obscured regarding what is wholesome and unwholesome;
it refers to one who concurrently cultivates the ten wholesome actions.
This is why retribution leads to birth in the heavens.
The Nine Sublime Precepts of the Daoists embody this very principle.
It is by means of these that humans plant the causes for becoming human.
The celestial vehicle can yield the fruit of heaven;
the worldly dharma is fundamentally rooted therein.
This is that which all three teachings equally attain.
As for the latter three vehicles,
they are intended to guide their followers to transcend and emerge from the mundane world,
causing them to forget both good and evil and proceed directly toward the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
When one attains spiritual penetration, the world cannot fathom such a person. Some,
however, merely observe that Gongsun Hong practiced "crooked learning" to curry favor with the age,
or that Zhu Qinming reduced the Five Classics to ruins.
Yang Xiong elucidated the subtleties of the *Taixuan* yet flattered the Han emperors;
Xu Jingzong understood the principles of the *Diqu* yet surrendered himself to the Empress Dowager.
Both of these men emerged from the Confucian school.
The Daoist Shu deceived Dongpo with the arts of the midnight hour;
Lin Lingsu deluded Emperor Huizong with dreams of the Shenxiao Heaven.
These "celestial immortals" were merely commoners in reality.
How could the subterranean immortals be one, when in reality they are but commoners?
All of these have emerged from the Daoist school.
The incantations and arts of the barbarian monks could not kill Fu Yi.
The stone Buddha manifesting light could not deceive Cheng Hao;
the Buddha’s tooth was miraculous, yet it was shattered by Fu Yi’s ram-horn saw;
the Buddha’s tooth was divine, yet it was destroyed by Zhao Feng’s axe and halberd.
All of these have emerged from within the Buddha's own school.
To view them cumulatively,
one sees that the three teachings have coexisted within China.
None of them have yet been able to emerge purely and entirely from the correct path;
so what is the point of fussing over such trivial distinctions of superiority and inferiority?
Furthermore, do they not consider that which I am discussing?
There are Confucians, Daoists, and Buddhists.
The Confucian teaches people through vigor, magnanimity, and integrity;
yet among those who profess to be Confucians, there are many whose actions deviate from the Way.
These are all criminals against the Confucian tradition.
The Way teaches people through purity and non-action;
yet those who profess the Way and instead devote themselves to heterodox arts—
These are all criminals against the Way of the Daoists.
The Buddha takes the preservation of life as his core principle;
he does not permit people to tread upon living grass with their feet.
How could one say that his teaching of incantations is for the purpose of killing people?
The Buddha takes formlessness as his fundamental principle;
the Tathāgata cannot be seen through physical marks.
Can it be said that he relied upon a stubborn stone to delude the masses?
Teeth may be broken,
but a stone is not a tooth.
They have fangs that can be destroyed;
they are counterfeit and not genuine.
All those who falsely claim affiliation with the teachings to create monsters and fabricate deceptions—
These are all culprits within the Buddha’s family.
How can one take such things as the basis for debating the Three Teachings?
Furthermore, some people pointlessly observe that the Daoist school possesses the *Huahu jing* (Scripture on Converting the Barbarians).
This refers to the claim that Śākyamuni and Mañjuśrī were actually transformed by Laozi and Yin Xi.
The Buddhist tradition possesses the *Poxie lun* (Treatise on Destroying Heresies).
This refers to the Buddha dispatching three disciples to transform and teach China:
Confucius was the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī (Rutong),
and Yan Hui was the Bodhisattva Vimalaprabha (Jingguang).
Laozi was none other than Mahākāśyapa. If this is indeed the case,
then how could the relative superiority or inferiority of the Three Teachings be easily established through mere casual conversation?
Little do they realize that the composition of these two works was each intended to exalt oneself and disparage the other.
Consequently, they ended up soaring on empty air while losing touch with reality.
Wang Fu composed the *Huahu jing* (Scripture on Laozi Converting the Barbarians),
claiming that Laozi and Yin Xi intended to convert the barbarians.
Upon attaining Buddhahood, he then transformed his body into that of Śākyamuni Mañjuśrī,
after which the Hu people were converted. Furthermore,
one must not fail to consider that the year of the Buddha’s birth was the twenty-fourth year of King Zhao of the Zhou dynasty.
The year of the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa was the fifty-second year of King Mu of Zhou.
Three hundred and forty-two years after the Buddha’s passing, during the reign of King Ding,
Laozi was born in Hu County of Chu.
When he served as an official under the pillars of King Zhou and passed through the Hangu Pass to meet Yin Xi,
more than four hundred years had already passed since the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa.
To employ the Way of later ages to transform oneself into a Buddha of former ages is precisely because the Way is insufficient to convert the Hu;
one must necessarily rely on the Buddha to convert the Hu.
Yang Su, the Minister of Works of the Sui dynasty, said:
"I have heard that when the Old Lord converted the Hu people,
they did not accept [his teachings]."
He then transformed his body along with Yin Xi into that of a Buddha so that the Hu people would finally accept him; had this been true,
it would mean that the Lord Lao was unable to convert the Hu.
It is well known that the Hu people have long been devoted to Buddhism.
Furthermore, Sengxun once said to the Daoist practitioners:
"Why did Laozi not convert the Hu to the Dao?"
What purpose is served by the transformation of the barbarians into Buddhists?
Is it not because the Daoist transformation fails to reach where the Buddhist transformation succeeds?
This is merely a frivolous theory intended to disparage the Buddha.
Little did they realize that this would, in fact, serve to honor the Buddha.
Falin composed the *Poxie lun* (Treatise on Destroying Heresies),
the general purport of which states:
Buddhism penetrates to the source of all phenomena,
whereas Confucianism and Daoism are merely systems for governing within this world;
it is said that [Buddhism] can thus dispel heterodox teachings and awaken the ignorant and benighted.
Furthermore, one must consider that Confucius and Yan Hui were certainly not bodhisattvas,
and Laozi was certainly not Kāśyapa; thus,
one seeks to correct those misrepresentations.
How could one possibly originate such a falsehood oneself?
Therefore, it cannot be said that there is too great an error in referring to Confucius and Yan Hui as bodhisattvas.
As for identifying Laozi as Kāśyapa,
this is a great error.
Kāśyapa received a distinct transmission of the teachings.
Following Śākyamuni to act as a patriarch,
he possessed at that time the wondrousness of the supreme vehicle, which cannot be transmitted through words; hundreds of thousands of beings,
both humans and devas, were formerly all at a loss as to how to grasp it.
Yet it was only Kāśyapa who attained it.
Could Laozi possibly have been a transformation of Kāśyapa?
Therefore, after Kāśyapa entrusted the Dharma to Ānanda, he entered meditative absorption on Mount Kukkuṭapāda.
He waited for the descent of Maitreya;
as long as Maitreya had not been born,
he did not emerge from that samādhi.
This Kāśyapa’s physical body remains in meditative concentration even now;
it is clear that he did not emerge as Laozi.
If one were to identify Kāśyapa with Laozi, [it would be a grave error].
Thus, to claim that Laozi was the ancestral patriarch of [Buddhism] is not it excessively erroneous?
Such is Lin’s argument, which effectively degrades the Way (Dao).
Yet one could not have anticipated that it would, in fact, serve to honor the Way.
These fabricated words are a gross distortion and falsehood.
What, then, does the discerning person take from this?
Furthermore, some merely observe the words of Master Yuancheng, who said:
"The words of Confucius and those of the Buddha—"
They serve as the beginning and end for one another.
Confucius and the Buddha were originally one;
it is only that their pedagogical methods and institutional arrangements differ.
Thus, the two teachings of Confucianism and Buddhism have never failed to accord with one another.
As the layman Guītáng said:
"The Buddha is the ultimate of human nature."
The Way is the ultimate of destiny.
When the two teachings stand in opposition yet mutually encompass one another,
the subtle mysteries of primordial nature and destiny will finally be perfected.
Thus, the two teachings of Confucianism and Daoism have never been different from Buddhism.
The poem of Master Fu says:
"The Daoist cap, the Confucian shoes, and the Buddhist *kāṣāya*."
To harmonize the three schools into one school means that these three teachings have never failed to converge as one;
yet now you alone exalt Buddhism while disparaging Confucianism and Daoism.
How could this be the intention of the former sages?
One simply fails to realize that the words of the former sages were merely their skillful means.
For when the Confucians obtain their time and put their Way into practice,
holding office and serving in government,
the scales of judgment— whether bestowing or withholding authority— all proceed from their hands.
